In mathematics, '''stochastic analysis on manifolds''' or '''stochastic differential geometry''' is the study of [[Stochastic calculus|stochastic analysis]] over [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifolds]]. It is therefore a synthesis of stochastic analysis (the extension of [[calculus]] to [[stochastic process]]es) and of [[differential geometry]].

The connection between [[Mathematical analysis|analysis]] and stochastic processes stems from the fundamental relation that the [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] of a continuous [[Strong Markov property|strong]] [[Markov chain|Markov process]] is a second-order [[Elliptic partial differential equation|elliptic operator]]. The infinitesimal generator of [[Brownian motion]] is the [[Laplace operator]] and the [[transition probability]] density <math>p(t,x,y)</math> of Brownian motion is the minimal [[heat kernel]] of the [[heat equation]]. Interpreting the paths of Brownian motion as [[Method of characteristics|characteristic curves]] of the operator, Brownian motion can be seen as a stochastic counterpart of a flow to a second-order partial differential operator.

Stochastic analysis on manifolds investigates stochastic processes on non-linear state spaces or [[Manifold|manifolds]]. Classical theory can be reformulated in a [[coordinate-free]] representation. In that, it is often complicated (or not possible) to formulate objects with coordinates of <math>\R^d</math>. Thus, we require an additional structure in form of a linear [[Connection (mathematics)|connection]] or [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian metric]] to define martingales and Brownian motion on manifolds. Therefore, controlled by the Riemannian metric, Brownian motion will be a local object by definition. However, its stochastic behaviour determines global aspects of the topology and geometry of the manifold.

Brownian motion is defined to be the [[diffusion process]] generated by the [[Laplace operators in differential geometry|Laplace-Beltrami operator]] <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta_M</math> with respect to a manifold <math>M</math> and can be constructed as the solution to a non-canonical [[stochastic differential equation]] on a Riemannian manifold. As there is no Hörmander representation of the operator <math>\Delta_M</math> if the manifold is not ''parallelizable'', i.e. if the [[tangent bundle]] is not trivial, there is no canonical procedure to construct Brownian motion. However, this obstacle can be overcome if the manifold is equipped with a connection: We can then introduce the ''stochastic horizontal lift'' of a [[semimartingale]] and the ''stochastic development'' by the so-called ''Eells-Elworthy-Malliavin construction''.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Stochastic differential equations on manifolds |date=1982 |volume=70}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Géométrie différentielle stochastique |date=1978}}</ref>

The latter is a generalisation of a [[horizontal lift]] of smooth curves to horizontal curves in the [[frame bundle]], such that the ''anti-development'' and the horizontal lift are connected by a stochastic differential equation. Using this, we can consider an SDE on the [[Frame bundle|orthonormal frame bundle]] of a [[Riemannian manifold]], whose solution is Brownian motion, and projects down to the (base) manifold via ''stochastic development''. A visual representation of this construction corresponds to the construction of a [[spherical Brownian motion]] by ''[[rolling without slipping]]'' the manifold along the paths (or footprints) of Brownian motion left in Euclidean space.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Stochastische Analysis: Eine Einführung in die Theorie der stetigen Semimartingale |date= |isbn=978-3-519-02229-9 |pages=349–544}}</ref>

Stochastic differential geometry provides insight into classical analytic problems, and offers new approaches to prove results by means of probability. For example, one can apply Brownian motion to the [[Dirichlet boundary condition|Dirichlet problem]] at infinity for [[Hadamard manifold|Cartan-Hadamard manifolds]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Neel |first1=Robert W. |title=Brownian Motion and the Dirichlet Problem at Infinity on Two-dimensional Cartan-Hadamard Manifolds |journal=Potential Analysis |date=2014 |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=443–462 |doi=10.1007/s11118-013-9376-3|arxiv=0912.0330 }}</ref> or give a probabilistic proof of the [[Atiyah–Singer index theorem|Atiyah-Singer index theorem]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=Stochastic Analysis on Manifolds |date= |volume=38}}</ref> Stochastic differential geometry also applies in other areas of mathematics (e.g. [[mathematical finance]]). For example, we can convert classical [[Arbitrage|arbitrage theory]] into differential-geometric language (also called ''[[geometric arbitrage theory]]'').<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Farinelli |first1=Simone |title=Geometric Arbitrage Theory and Market Dynamics |journal=Journal of Geometric Mechanics |date=2015 |volume=7 |doi=10.3934/jgm.2015.7.431 |issue=4 |pages=431–471 |doi-access=free |arxiv=0910.1671 }}</ref>

== Preface ==
{{research paper|section|date=July 2025}}
For the reader's convenience and if not stated otherwise, let <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{A},(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\geq 0},\mathbb P)</math> be a [[Filtration (probability theory)|filtered]] [[probability space]] and <math>M</math> be a smooth manifold. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions, i.e. it is [[right-continuous]] and complete. We use the [[Stratonovich integral]] which obeys the classical [[chain rule]] (compared to [[Itô calculus]]). The main advantage for us lies in the fact that stochastic differential equations are then stable under [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphisms]] <math>f:M\to N</math> between manifolds, i.e. if <math>X</math> is a solution, then also <math>f(X)</math> is a solution under transformations of the stochastic differential equation.

Notation:

* <math>TM</math> is. the [[tangent bundle]] of <math>M</math>.
* <math>T^*M</math> is the [[Tangent bundle|cotangent bundle]] of <math>M</math>.
* <math>\Gamma(TM)</math> is the <math>C^{\infty}(M)</math>-module of [[vector fields]] on <math>M</math>.
* <math>X \circ dZ</math> is the Stratonovich integral.
* <math>C^{\infty}_c(M)</math> is the space of [[test functions]] on <math>M</math>, i.e. <math>f\in C^{\infty}_c(M)</math> is smooth and has compact support.
* <math>\widehat{M}:=M\cup \{\infty\}</math> is the [[Alexandroff extension|one-point compactification]] (or Alexandroff compactification).

== Flow processes ==
''Flow processes'' (also called <math>L</math>''-diffusions'') are the probabilistic counterpart of [[Integral curve|integral curves]] ([[Flow (mathematics)|flow lines]]) of vector fields. In contrast, a flow process is defined with respect to a [[Second-order differential equation|second-order differential operator]], and thus, generalises the notion of deterministic flows being defined with respect to a [[First order differential equation|first-order operator]].

=== Partial differential operator in Hörmander form ===
Let <math>A\in \Gamma(TM)</math> be a vector field, understood as a derivation by the <math>C^{\infty}(M)</math>-[[isomorphism]]

: <math>\Gamma(TM)\to \operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{R}} C^{\infty}(M),\quad A\mapsto (f\mapsto Af)</math>

for some <math>f\in C^{\infty}(M)</math>. The map <math>Af:M\to \mathbb{R}</math> is defined by <math>Af(x):=A_x(f)</math>. For the composition, we set <math>A^2:=A(A(f))</math> for some <math>f\in C^{\infty}(M)</math>.

A [[Differential operator|partial differential operator]] (PDO) <math>L:C^{\infty}(M)\to C^{\infty}(M)</math> is given in ''Hörmander form'' if and only there are vector fields <math>A_0,A_1,\dots,A_r\in \Gamma(TM)</math> and <math>L</math> can be written in the form

: <math>L=A_0+\sum\limits_{i=1}^r A_i^2</math>.

=== Flow process ===
Let <math>L</math> be a PDO in Hörmander form on <math>M</math> and <math>x\in M</math> a starting point. An adapted and continuous <math>M</math>-valued process <math>X</math> with <math>X_0=x</math> is called a ''flow process to <math>L</math> starting in <math>x</math>'', if for every test function <math>f\in C^{\infty}_c(M)</math> and <math>t\in\mathbb{R}_+</math> the process

: <math>N(f)_t:=f(X_t)-f(X_0)-\int_0^t Lf(X_r)\mathrm{d}r </math>

is a martingale, i.e.

: <math>\mathbb{E}\left(N(f)_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s\right)=N(f)_s,\quad \forall s\leq t</math>.

=== Remark ===
For a test function <math>f\in C^{\infty}_c(M)</math>, a PDO <math>L</math> in Hörmander form and a flow process <math>X_t^x</math> (starting in <math>x</math>) also holds the flow equation, but in comparison to the deterministic case ''only in mean''

: <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E} f(X_t^x) = \mathbb{E}\left[Lf(X_t^x)\right]</math>.

and we can recover the PDO by taking the [[time derivative]] at time 0, i.e. 

: <math>\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{t=0}\mathbb{E}f(X_t^x)=Lf(x)</math>.

=== Lifetime and explosion time ===
Let <math>\empty \neq U\subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> be open und <math>\xi>0</math> a predictable [[stopping time]]. We call <math>\xi</math> the ''lifetime'' of a continuous semimartingale <math>X=(X_t)_{0\leq t<\xi}</math> on <math>U</math> if

* there is a sequence of stopping times <math>(\xi_n)</math> with <math>\xi_n\nearrow\xi</math>, such that <math>\xi_n< \xi</math> <math>\mathbb P</math>-almost surely on <math>\{0<\xi<\infty\}</math>.
* the stopped process <math>(X_{t\wedge \xi_n})</math> is a semimartingale.

Moreover, if <math>X_{\xi_n(\omega)}\to \partial U</math> for almost all <math>\omega\in\{\xi<\infty\}</math>, we call <math>\xi</math> ''explosion time''.

A flow process <math>X</math> can have a finite lifetime <math>\xi</math>. By this we mean that <math>X=(X)_{t<\xi}</math> is defined such that if <math>t\to \xi</math>, then <math>\mathbb P</math>-almost surely on <math>\{\xi<\infty\}</math> we have <math>X_t\to \infty</math> in the one-point compactification <math>\widehat{M}:=M\cup \{\infty\}</math>. In that case we extend the process path-wise by <math>X_t:=\infty</math> for <math>t\geq \xi</math>.

=== Semimartingales on a manifold ===
A process <math>X</math> is a s''emimartingale on <math>M</math>'', if for every <math>f\in C^2(M)</math> the random variable <math>f(X)</math> is an <math>\R</math>-semimartingale, i.e. the composition of any smooth function <math>f</math> with the process <math>X</math> is a real-valued semimartingale. It can be shown that any <math>M</math>-semimartingale is a solution of a stochastic differential equation on <math>M</math>. If the semimartingale is only defined up to a finite lifetime <math>\xi</math>, we can always construct a semimartingale with infinite lifetime by a transformation of time. A semimartingale has a quadratic variation with respect to a section in the bundle of [[Bilinear form|bilinear forms]] on <math>TM</math>.

Introducing the ''Stratonovich Integral of a [[differential form]] <math>\alpha</math> along the semimartingale <math>X</math>'' we can study the so called ''winding behaviour'' of <math>X</math>, i.e. a generalisation of the [[winding number]].

=== Stratonovich integral of a 1-form ===
Let <math>X</math> be an <math>M</math>-valued semimartingale and <math>\alpha\in\Gamma(T^*M)</math> be a [[1-form]]. We call the integral <math>\int_X\alpha:=\int \alpha (\circ dX)</math> the ''Stratonovich integral of <math>\alpha</math> along <math>X</math>''. For <math>f\in C^{\infty}(M)</math> we define <math>f(X)\circ \alpha(\circ dX):=f(X)\circ d(\int_X\alpha)</math>.

== SDEs on a manifold<span class="anchor" id="Stochastic differential equations on manifolds"></span> ==
A ''stochastic differential equation on a manifold'' <math>M</math>, denoted ''SDE on <math>M</math>'', is defined by the pair <math>(A,Z)</math> including a bundle homomorphism (i.e. a ''homomorphism of vector bundles'') or the (<math>r+1</math>)-tuple <math>(A_1,\dots,A_r,Z)</math> with vector fields <math>A_1,\dots,A_r</math> given. Using the [[Whitney embedding theorem|Whitney embedding]], we can show that there is a unique maximal solution to every SDE on <math>M</math> with [[initial condition]] <math>X_0=x</math>. If we have identified the maximal solution, we recover directly a flow process <math>X^x</math> to the operator <math>L</math>.

=== Definition ===
An ''SDE on <math>M</math>'' is a pair <math>(A,Z)</math>, where

* <math>Z=(Z_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}_+}</math> is a continuous semimartingale on a finite-dimensional <math>\R</math>-[[vector space]] <math>E</math>; and
* <math>A:M\times E\to TM</math> is a (smooth) [[homomorphism]] of [[Vector bundle|vector bundles]] over <math>M</math>

: <math>A:(x,e)\mapsto A(x)e</math>

where<math>A(x):E\to TM</math> is a linear map.

The stochastic differential equation <math>(A,Z)</math> is denoted by

: <math>dX=A(X)\circ dZ</math>

or

: <math>dX=\sum\limits_{i=1}^r A_i(X)\circ dZ^i.</math>

The latter follows from setting <math>A_i:=A(\cdot)e_i</math> with respect to a basis <math>(e_i)_{i=1,\dots,r}</math> and <math>\R</math>-valued semimartingales <math>(Z^{i})_{i=1,\dots,r}</math> with <math>Z=\sum\limits_{i=1}^rZ^{i}e_i</math>.

As for given vector fields <math>A_1,\dots,A_r\in \Gamma(TM)</math> there is exactly one bundle homomorphism <math>A</math> such that <math>A_i:=A(\cdot)e_i</math>, our definition of an SDE on <math>M</math> as <math>(A_1,\dots,A_r,Z)</math> is plausible.

If <math>Z</math> has only finite life time, we can transform the time horizon into the infinite case.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Stochastische Analysis: Eine Einführung in die Theorie der stetigen Semimartingale |isbn=978-3-519-02229-9 |pages=364}}</ref>

=== Solutions<span class="anchor" id="Solutions to SDEs on a manifold"></span> ===
Let <math>(A,Z)</math> be an SDE on <math>M</math> and <math>x_0:\Omega\to M</math> an <math>\mathcal{F}_0</math>-measurable [[random variable]]. Let <math>(X_t)_{t<\zeta}</math> be a continuous adapted <math>M</math>-valued process with life time <math>\zeta</math> on the same probability space such as <math>Z</math>. Then <math>(X_t)_{t<\zeta}</math> is called a ''solution'' to the SDE

: <math>dX=A(X)\circ dZ</math>

with initial condition <math>X_0=x_0</math> up to the life time <math>\zeta</math>, if for every test function <math>f \in C^{\infty}_c(M)</math> the process <math>f(X)</math> is an <math>\R</math>-valued semimartingale and for every stopping time <math>\tau</math> with <math>0\leq \tau < \zeta</math>, it holds <math>\mathbb P</math>-almost surely

: <math>f(X_\tau) = f(x_0) + \int_0^\tau (df)_{X_s} A(X_s)\circ \mathrm{d}Z_s </math>,

where <math>(df)_X:T_xM\to T_{f(x)}M</math> is the [[Pushforward (differential)|push-forward]] (or differential) at the point <math>X</math>. Following the idea from above, by definition <math>f(X)</math> is a semimartingale for every test function <math>f\in C_c^{\infty}(M)</math>, so that <math>X</math> is a ''semimartingale on <math>M</math>''. 

If the lifetime is maximal, i.e.

: <math>\{\zeta <\infty\}\subset\left\{\lim\limits_{t\nearrow \zeta}X_t=\infty \text{ in }\widehat{M}\right\}</math>

<math>\mathbb P</math>-almost surely, we call this solution the ''maximal solution''. The lifetime of a maximal solution <math>X</math> can be extended to all of <math>\R_+</math> , and after extending <math>f</math> to the whole of <math>\widehat{M}</math>, the equation

: <math>f(X_{t})=f(X_0)+\int_0^t (df)_X A(X)\circ dZ, \quad t\geq 0</math>,

holdsup to indistinguishability.<ref>{{citation|author=Wolfgang Hackenbroch und Anton Thalmaier|editor=Vieweg+Teubner Verlag Wiesbaden|isbn=978-3-519-02229-9|pages=364|title=Stochastische Analysis: Eine Einführung in die Theorie der stetigen Semimartingale}}<!-- auto-translated by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>

=== Remark ===
Let <math>Z=(t,B)</math> with a <math>d</math>-dimensional Brownian motion <math>B=(B_1,\dots,B_d)</math>, then we can show that every maximal solution starting in <math>x_0</math> is a flow process to the operator

: <math>L=A_0+\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^d A_i^2</math>.

== Martingales and Brownian motion ==
Brownian motion on manifolds are stochastic flow processes to the [[Laplace operators in differential geometry|Laplace-Beltrami operator]]. It is possible to construct Brownian motion on [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian manifolds]] <math>(M,g)</math>. However, to follow a canonical [[ansatz]], we need some additional structure. Let <math>\mathcal{O}(d)</math> be the [[orthogonal group]]; we consider the canonical SDE on the [[Frame bundle|orthonormal frame bundle]] <math>O(M)</math> over <math>M</math>, whose solution is Brownian motion. The orthonormal frame bundle is the collection of all sets <math>O_x(M)</math> of [[Frame bundle|orthonormal frames]] of the tangent space <math>T_xM</math>

: <math>O(M):=\bigcup\limits_{x\in M}O_x(M)</math>

or in other words, the <math>\mathcal{O}(d)</math>-[[principal bundle]] associated to <math>TM</math>.
[[File:Eells-Elworthy-Malliavin-construction.jpg|thumb|The Eells-Elworthy-Malliavin construction of the Brownian motion on manifolds]]
Let <math>W</math> be an <math>\R^d</math>-valued semimartingale. The solution <math>U</math> of the SDE

: <math>dU_t = \sum\limits_{i=1}^d A_i(U_t)\circ dW_t^i,\quad U_0=u_0,</math>

defined by the projection <math>\pi:O(M)\to M</math> of a Brownian motion <math>X</math> on the Riemannian manifold, is the ''stochastic development'' from <math>W</math> on <math>M</math>. Conversely we call <math>W</math> the ''anti-development'' of <math>U</math> or, respectively, <math>\pi(U)=X</math>. In short, we get the following relations: <math>W\leftrightarrow U \leftrightarrow X</math>, where

* <math>U</math> is an <math>O(M)</math>-valued semimartingale; and
* <math>X</math> is an <math>M</math>-valued semimartingale.

For a Riemannian manifold we always use the [[Levi-Civita connection]] and the corresponding Laplace-Beltrami operator <math>\Delta_M</math>. The key observation is that there exists a lifted version of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on the orthonormal frame bundle. The fundamental relation reads, for <math>f\in C^{\infty}(M)</math>,

: <math>\Delta_M f(x)=\Delta_{O(M)}(f\circ \pi)(u)</math>

for all <math>u\in O(M)</math> with <math>\pi u=x</math>, and the operator <math>\Delta_{O(M)}</math> on <math>O(M)</math> is well-defined for so-called ''horizontal vector fields''. The operator <math>\Delta_{O(M)}</math> is called ''Bochner's horizontal Laplace operator''.

=== Martingales with linear connection ===
To define martingales, we need a linear connection <math>\nabla</math>. Using the connection, we can characterise <math>\nabla</math>-martingales, if their anti-development is a local martingale. It is also possible to define <math>\nabla</math>-martingales without using the anti-development.

We write <math>\stackrel{m}{=}</math> to indicate that equality holds [[Euclidean division|modulo]] differentials of [[Local martingale|local martingales]].

Let <math>X</math> be an <math>M</math>-valued semimartingale. Then <math>X</math> is a ''martingale'' or ''<math>\nabla</math>-martingale'', if and only if for every <math>f\in C^{\infty}(M)</math>, it holds that

: <math>d(f\circ X)\,\,\stackrel{m}{=}\,\,\tfrac{1}{2}(\nabla df)(dX,dX).</math>

=== Brownian motion on a Riemannian manifold ===
Let <math>(M,g)</math> be a [[Riemannian manifold]] with Laplace-Beltrami operator <math>\Delta_{M}</math>. An adapted <math>M</math>-valued process <math>X</math> with maximal lifetime <math>\xi</math> is called a ''Brownian motion<math>(M,g)</math>'', if for every <math>f\in C^{\infty}(M)</math>

: <math>f(X)-\frac{1}{2}\int\Delta_{M} f(X)\mathrm{d}t</math>

is a local <math>\R</math>-martingale with life time <math>\xi</math>. Hence, Brownian motion Bewegung is the diffusion process to <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta_{M}</math>. Note that this characterisation does not provide a canonical procedure to define Brownian motion.
